sections.name: General Knowledge
sections.note: Part 1 (VALR, DM, QADI) shares a combined 170-minute limit; GK is a separate 10-minute section with no negative marking.

items.set_title: RC7: The Quiet Power of Maintenance
items.passage: Societies celebrate builders and inventors, and forget maintainers. Yet most of what makes daily life work is maintenance: the engineer who keeps the water system running, the nurse who notices a change before it becomes a crisis, the teacher who repairs a misunderstanding before it hardens into failure. Maintenance is invisible when it succeeds, which is why it is undervalued. A bridge that does not collapse earns no ceremony; a system that never breaks down wins no prize. Funding follows the same bias. New projects attract ribbon-cuttings and headlines, while the budget to keep old systems working is cut quietly, year after year, until a failure forces attention. The result is a cycle of neglect and emergency: starve the routine, pay extravagantly for the crisis. Breaking the cycle requires seeing maintenance as creative work, not as the absence of innovation. Keeping a complex system alive under changing conditions demands judgement, improvisation and deep knowledge. A society that honours only the new will keep rebuilding what it failed to maintain.
items.question: The passage argues that maintenance is undervalued because
options: it is invisible when it succeeds
items.explanation: The passage states maintenance is invisible when it succeeds, which is why it is undervalued. It stresses maintenance demands judgement and knowledge, so lack of skill is false, and refusal or cheapness is not the reason.

items.set_title: RC7: The Quiet Power of Maintenance
items.question: The cycle described in the passage is
options: starve routine upkeep, then pay extravagantly for crisis
items.explanation: The passage names the cycle as starve the routine and pay extravagantly for the crisis. The other sequences do not match the text.

items.set_title: RC7: The Quiet Power of Maintenance
items.question: The author would describe keeping a complex system alive as
options: a task that needs no knowledge
creative work requiring judgement and improvisation
items.explanation: The passage says maintenance is creative work demanding judgement, improvisation and deep knowledge. The other options contradict that characterisation.

items.set_title: RC7: The Quiet Power of Maintenance
items.question: Which policy would the author most likely support?
options: Cutting maintenance budgets to fund new projects
Waiting for failures before spending on systems
Funding steady upkeep even without ceremonies or headlines
items.explanation: The author criticises cutting upkeep quietly and the neglect-emergency cycle, so steady upkeep funding follows. The other options are the practices criticised.

items.passage: Organisations say they learn from failure, but most do the opposite: they hide it, punish it, or explain it away. The reason is not dishonesty alone. Failure threatens identity. A team that prides itself on excellence hears a failed project as an accusation, and a manager whose promotion depends on clean results has every reason to bury bad news. Yet without an honest account of what went wrong, the same mistakes repeat under new names. Learning requires a different response: separate the person from the problem, describe what happened in plain language, and ask what the system allowed to happen rather than who should be blamed. This is harder than it sounds, because it asks leaders to reward candour that makes them look bad in the short term. The organisations that manage it share a habit: they review failures quickly, while memories are fresh, and they write down what will change, with a name and a date attached. The review is not a ritual of apology. It is a mechanism for turning an expensive event into usable knowledge.
items.question: According to the passage, organisations often fail to learn from failure because
options: failure is rare in well-run firms
failures are too complex to describe
failure threatens identity and incentives reward hiding it
items.explanation: The passage says failure threatens identity and managers with promotion tied to clean results have reason to bury bad news. Rarity, enjoyment and indescribability are not given as reasons.

items.question: The author recommends separating the person from the problem in order to
options: focus on what the system allowed to happen
items.explanation: The passage says separate the person from the problem and ask what the system allowed to happen rather than who should be blamed. Avoiding all punishment and protecting managers are not the stated purpose.

items.question: Which practice is characteristic of organisations that learn from failure?
options: Waiting until memories fade before reviewing
Holding reviews as rituals of apology
Reviewing failures quickly and recording changes with a name and date
items.explanation: The passage lists quick reviews while memories are fresh and written changes with a name and date. Waiting, apology rituals and public blame are the opposite of the recommended habit.

items.question: The author's view of a failure review is that it should be
options: a mechanism for turning an expensive event into usable knowledge
a private matter never written down
items.explanation: The closing sentence defines the review as a mechanism for turning an expensive event into usable knowledge. Blame, secrecy and reputation protection contradict the argument.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to TRANQUIL.
items.explanation: Tranquil means calm and peaceful, so turbulent is the opposite. Peaceful, calm and serene are synonyms.

items.question: Fill in the blank: The contract was ______ after both parties agreed to the revised terms.
items.explanation: Agreeing to revised terms leads to formal approval, so ratified fits. Disputed and ignored contradict agreement, and postponed suggests no agreement was reached.

items.question: Identify the sentence with NO error.
options: The numbers of applicants has increased.
The number of applicant has increased.
The number of applicants has increased.
The number of applicants have increased.
items.explanation: The number is singular and takes has, and applicants is the correct plural noun. Have mismatches the singular subject, numbers with has mismatches, and applicant should be plural.

items.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
items.explanation: The correct spelling is separate, with a after p and a after r. The other forms use e in the wrong places.

items.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
items.explanation: The correct spelling is harassment, with one r and double s. The other forms add or drop letters incorrectly.

items.question: Which sentence is the best paraphrase of 'The policy failed not because it was unpopular, but because it was poorly implemented'?
options: The cause of failure was poor implementation, not unpopularity
The policy was popular but badly run
The policy failed because people disliked it
The policy was unpopular and badly run
items.explanation: The original contrasts unpopularity with poor implementation and blames the latter, which the third option restates exactly. The other options misassign the cause.

items.question: Statement: If it rains, the match will be cancelled. It did not rain. What can be concluded?
options: Nothing certain can be concluded about the match
items.explanation: Denying the antecedent does not prove the consequent is false; the match could still be cancelled for another reason or held. Only the third option respects that logic.

items.question: All cats are mammals. Some mammals are black. Therefore:
items.explanation: Some mammals are black directly gives some black animals are mammals, since black mammals are black animals. The overlap need not include cats, so the cat conclusions do not follow.

items.question: Choose the analogy: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
items.explanation: A doctor works in a hospital, and a teacher works in a school. Student is the recipient, book is a tool, and lesson is the activity, not the workplace.

items.question: Choose the analogy: Pen : Write :: Knife : ?
items.explanation: A pen is used to write and a knife is used to cut, which is the function relation. Sharp is a property, kitchen is a place, and metal is a material.

items.question: Find the odd one out.
items.explanation: Mumbai, Delhi and Chennai are cities, while Ganga is a river. The first three share the category of city, and Ganga belongs to a different category.

items.question: Find the odd one out.
items.explanation: Square, circle and triangle are two-dimensional shapes, while a cube is three-dimensional. The dimensional difference makes cube the odd one out.

items.question: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to burn the midnight oil'.
options: To work late into the night
items.explanation: Burning the midnight oil means working or studying late into the night. It is not about wasting fuel, starting fires or cooking.

items.question: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'once in a blue moon'.
items.explanation: Once in a blue moon means very rarely. It does not mean monthly, at night generally, or during a festival.

items.question: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to spill the beans'.
items.explanation: To spill the beans means to reveal secret information. It is not about cooking, wasting food or dropping objects.

items.question: Fill in the blank: The new manager's ______ approach won the trust of a team that had seen three leaders in two years.
items.explanation: A team that has seen frequent leadership change would trust a steady approach. Erratic, aloof and hasty would undermine trust rather than win it.

items.question: Fill in the blank: The evidence was ______; it pointed clearly to a single conclusion.
items.explanation: Evidence pointing clearly to a single conclusion is unequivocal. Ambiguous, inconclusive and contradictory all imply uncertainty or conflict.

items.question: Which statement is an assumption of the argument 'We must build more hostels because students cannot find affordable rooms'?
options: Building hostels will provide affordable rooms for students
Students want to live near campus
Hostels are better than rented rooms
items.explanation: The argument assumes building hostels will actually provide the affordable rooms students lack. Wanting to live near campus and preferring hostels are not required, and all students being poor is far stronger than needed.

items.passage: A firm can move a factory to a region with lower wages, saving costs and keeping prices low for customers. The move will end 300 local jobs in a town where the factory is the largest employer. The board is split between cost competitiveness and community responsibility.
items.question: Which consideration should the board weigh most carefully?
options: The long-term cost of losing skilled workers and community trust versus the wage saving
The colour of the new factory
items.explanation: Losing skilled workers and community trust can erase the wage saving over time through hiring, training and reputational costs. Press wording, factory colour and travel time are trivial beside livelihoods and capability.

items.question: A phased relocation with retraining and a transition fund is preferable to an abrupt move because it
options: reduces harm to workers and preserves skills the firm may still need
items.explanation: Phasing with retraining and a fund reduces harm and preserves skills, even though it costs money and does not guarantee zero losses or please everyone. The benefit is mitigation, not elimination of all cost or conflict.

items.question: What should the firm do for the affected town?
options: Promise the factory will never close
Blame the town for high wages
Engage the local community early, share the timeline, and support redeployment or new employers
items.explanation: Early engagement, a shared timeline and redeployment support treat the town as a stakeholder rather than an afterthought. Leaving without notice, blaming the town and false promises all damage trust and the firm's standing.

items.passage: A brand is offered a promotion by a popular online creator whose audience matches its customers. The creator has previously promoted a rival's faulty product without disclosing payment. The brand's marketing team loves the reach; the legal team worries about disclosure and credibility.
items.question: What should the brand require before signing?
options: A promise the creator will never promote rivals again
No conditions, to keep the creator happy
Payment in advance with no review
A written disclosure agreement, a factual claim check, and the right to review claims before publication
items.explanation: Written disclosure, factual checks and pre-publication review directly address the creator's history of undisclosed promotion. No conditions, advance payment without review and a non-compete promise do not fix disclosure or accuracy.

items.question: The creator's past undisclosed promotion matters because it
options: means the creator has no audience
shows a pattern that could transfer distrust to the brand
is irrelevant once a new contract is signed
items.explanation: A pattern of undisclosed promotion signals the brand's claims may also be presented without disclosure, transferring distrust. Popularity, contract novelty and audience size do not erase that pattern.

items.question: If the creator refuses disclosure, the brand should
options: Double the fee to change the creator's mind
Walk away, since undisclosed promotion risks regulatory action and trust loss
items.explanation: Walking away avoids regulatory and trust risks that reach cannot offset. Proceeding, doubling the fee and hiding payment all accept the very practice the legal team flagged.

items.passage: A small supplier signed a five-year fixed-price contract with a large buyer. Raw material prices have since doubled, so every delivery now loses money. The buyer insists on the contract terms. The supplier can breach the contract and face legal action, absorb losses until bankruptcy, or ask to renegotiate.
items.question: What should the supplier do first?
options: Ask to renegotiate, presenting cost evidence and options such as phased increases or reduced volumes
items.explanation: Asking to renegotiate with cost evidence and options gives the buyer a reasoned basis to share the burden. Silent breach, stopping deliveries and unilateral rises all break trust and invite legal action without a hearing.

items.question: The buyer's insistence on the terms is understandable but incomplete because
options: a bankrupt supplier cannot deliver at all, so strict enforcement may destroy the supply the buyer needs
items.explanation: Strict enforcement that bankrupts the supplier destroys the very supply the buyer relies on, so the buyer's long-term interest may favour renegotiation. Contracts do matter, the supplier is not automatically right, and prices do rise.

items.question: What clause would have prevented this dispute?
options: A price-adjustment clause linked to an input cost index, with caps and review triggers
A clause requiring the supplier to absorb all losses
items.explanation: An index-linked adjustment with caps and triggers shares input-cost risk fairly instead of loading it all on one party. A ban, an absorb-all clause and no contract all leave the risk unmanaged.

items.passage: A school has one seat left and two applicants. One scored slightly higher on the entrance test; the other comes from a disadvantaged background and scored slightly lower but overcame far greater obstacles. The school's published rule is strictly merit by test score, but its mission statement emphasises widening access.
items.question: What is the core conflict?
options: A published merit rule versus a mission to widen access
items.explanation: The conflict is between the published strictly merit rule and the mission to widen access, which point to different applicants. Test versus interview, identical scores and parents versus teachers are not the tension described.

items.question: What process best resolves the conflict fairly?
options: Apply the published rule for this seat, and review the rule openly for future admissions
Change the rule retroactively for this seat without notice
Decide secretly by the head's preference
Give the seat to whoever applies first
items.explanation: Applying the published rule now preserves trust in stated criteria, while an open review for the future addresses the mission tension honestly. Secret choice, retroactive change and first-come allocation all undermine fairness or transparency.

items.question: If the school changes its rule for the future, it should
options: Change it every year without notice
Apply it silently to selected applicants
Announce the change before the next admission cycle with clear criteria
Keep the old rule published while using a new one
items.explanation: Announcing before the next cycle with clear criteria lets future applicants plan and holds the school accountable. Silent, dual-rule and unannounced annual changes all mislead applicants.

items.passage: A project is 30 percent over budget with two months left. The project head can cut testing to finish on budget, ask for more funds with a revised plan, or reduce the project's scope in agreement with the client. Cutting testing risks defects; asking for funds risks the client's trust; reducing scope risks disappointing users.
items.question: What should the project head do?
options: Cut testing quietly to stay on budget
Blame the team for the overrun
Present the client with the true position, the options, and a recommendation, and agree the path forward
items.explanation: Presenting the true position with options and a recommendation lets the client choose knowingly between testing, funds and scope. Quiet cuts, hiding and blame all deprive the client of a decision they own.

items.question: Cutting testing is the riskiest option because
options: defects found by users cost more in fixes, reputation and rework than testing would have cost
items.explanation: Defects reaching users cost more in fixes, reputation and rework than the testing saved, so the apparent saving is false economy. Testing is not free, clients do notice defects, and testing does find issues.

items.question: What should the project head do to prevent a repeat?
options: Track costs weekly against a baseline, with early warning triggers and a change process
items.explanation: Weekly tracking against a baseline with early warnings and a change process catches overruns while they are still manageable. Not reporting, promising lower budgets and avoiding risk all leave the cause untouched.

items.passage: A procurement officer is preparing a tender for road repairs. A contractor casually mentions details of the evaluation criteria that have not yet been published, and offers the officer a consultancy fee to keep the process smooth. The officer suspects the contractor learned the criteria from a colleague. Cancelling the tender would delay the repairs by six months.
items.question: What should the officer do first?
options: Quietly change the criteria so the contractor's knowledge is useless
Warn the contractor to keep quiet and carry on
Report the approach and the suspected leak to the vigilance unit and record the conversation
Accept the fee but award the tender fairly anyway
items.explanation: The officer must report both the bribe attempt and the leak through the proper channel and create a record. Accepting money is corruption even if the award is fair, silently changing criteria hides a leak that should be investigated, and warning the contractor protects the wrongdoing.

items.question: Cancelling the tender is costly, but proceeding as planned is worse because
options: A compromised tender destroys trust in the whole process and invites legal challenge
The evaluation criteria are too complicated
The contractor is the cheapest bidder available
Road repairs are less important than other projects
items.explanation: A tender known to be compromised cannot produce a defensible result. Losing bidders can challenge it, and public trust in the process collapses. Delay is a real cost, but it is smaller than a corrupt award that must later be undone.

items.question: What process change best prevents a repeat?
options: Ban contractors from talking to procurement staff
Increase the number of bidders invited
Restrict access to draft criteria and publish them simultaneously to all bidders
Make the tender period shorter so leaks have less time
items.explanation: Leaks happen when drafts circulate widely and reach some bidders early. Restricting access and publishing criteria to everyone at the same moment removes the advantage. Shorter periods, conversation bans and more bidders do not fix the information asymmetry.

items.passage: A bank branch manager faces pressure to waive a small farmer's overdue loan after a crop failure, although the bank's policy allows waivers only for documented natural calamities and the farmer's papers are incomplete. Other borrowers are watching, and a waiver without papers may set a precedent.
items.question: What should the manager do?
options: Help the farmer complete the documentation, verify the crop failure, and then apply the policy fairly
Refuse and seize the farmer's assets immediately
Waive the loan secretly and tell no one
Waive the loan at once without papers
items.explanation: Helping with documentation and verifying the failure lets the manager apply the policy fairly instead of breaking it or refusing a genuine case. Immediate waiver, seizure and secret waiver all ignore verification or precedent.

items.question: The precedent concern is valid because
options: a waiver without verification signals that rules can be bypassed, encouraging similar requests
other borrowers will never need waivers
items.explanation: An unverified waiver signals rules can be bypassed, which invites similar requests and undermines the policy. Other borrowers may need waivers, farmers do not always repay, and policies do change.

items.question: What would make the waiver decision most defensible?
options: A waiver granted only to borrowers who complain loudly
A private decision with no record
A written record of the evidence, the policy clause applied, and the reasoning
A decision based on the farmer's popularity
items.explanation: A written record of evidence, policy clause and reasoning makes the decision reviewable and consistent. Private, popularity-based and complaint-driven decisions cannot be defended to other borrowers.

items.question: What is 20% of 350?
items.explanation: 20% of 350 is 350 x 20/100 = 70. Ten percent is 35, so twenty percent is twice that, 70.

items.question: What is the greatest common divisor of 48 and 60?
items.explanation: The common divisors of 48 and 60 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, so the greatest is 12.

items.question: What is the perimeter of a square of side 9 cm?
items.explanation: Perimeter is 4 x side = 4 x 9 = 36 cm. A square has four equal sides, so the perimeter is four times one side, not the area 81.

items.question: What is the average of 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24?
items.explanation: The sum is 80 and there are 5 numbers, so the average is 80/5 = 16. The numbers are symmetric around 16, which is why the average is the middle value.

items.question: The ratio of income to expenditure is 5:4. If the savings are Rs 5000, what is the income?
items.explanation: One ratio part equals the savings of Rs 5000, so the income of 5 parts is 5 x 5000 = Rs 25000.

items.question: A can finish a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. Working together, how many days will they take?
items.explanation: Together they do 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 of the job per day, so they take 12 days. Rates add when people work together, but times do not.

items.question: A train 150 metres long running at 36 km/h crosses a pole. How long does it take?
items.explanation: 36 km/h is 10 m/s, so the time is 150/10 = 15 seconds. Converting km/h to m/s means multiplying by 5/18, and 36 x 5/18 = 10.

items.question: What is the compound interest on Rs 5000 for 2 years at 8% per annum?
items.explanation: The amount is 5000 x 1.08 x 1.08 = Rs 5832, so the interest is 5832 - 5000 = Rs 832.

items.question: A man buys an article for Rs 400 and sells it for Rs 340. What is his loss percentage?
items.explanation: The loss is 400 - 340 = Rs 60 on a cost of Rs 400, so 60/400 x 100 = 15%. Loss percentage is always calculated on the cost price, not the selling price.

items.question: A boat goes downstream at 15 km/h and upstream at 9 km/h. What is the speed of the stream?
items.explanation: The stream speed is half the difference of downstream and upstream speeds, (15 - 9)/2 = 3 km/h.

items.question: If x^2 - 9x + 20 = 0, what is the larger root?
items.explanation: The equation factors as (x - 4)(x - 5) = 0, so the roots are 4 and 5, and the larger is 5.

items.question: In a geometric progression 2, 4, 8, 16, ... what is the 6th term?
items.explanation: The common ratio is 2, so the 6th term is 2 x 2^5 = 64. Each term doubles the previous one: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.

items.question: Two coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
items.explanation: The outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT, and three of the four have at least one head, so the probability is 3/4.

items.question: A circle has diameter 28 cm. What is its circumference? (Use pi = 22/7)
items.explanation: Circumference is pi x diameter = (22/7) x 28 = 88 cm. The diameter 28 cancels the 7 in pi, giving 22 x 4 = 88.

items.question: What is the remainder when 2^50 is divided by 5?
items.explanation: Modulo 5, powers of 2 cycle 2, 4, 3, 1 with period 4. Since 50 leaves remainder 2 on division by 4, 2^50 is congruent to 4.

items.question: In how many ways can 5 people be seated around a circular table?
items.explanation: Circular arrangements of n people number (n - 1)! = 4! = 24, because rotations of the same seating are identical.

items.question: A parallelogram has base 12 cm and height 8 cm. What is its area?
items.explanation: Area is base x height = 12 x 8 = 96 sq cm. A parallelogram has the same area as a rectangle with the same base and height.

items.question: If a + b = 7 and ab = 10, what is the value of a^2 + b^2?
items.explanation: a^2 + b^2 = (a + b)^2 - 2ab = 49 - 20 = 29. Squaring the sum introduces the cross term 2ab, which must be subtracted to isolate the squares.

items.question: A car travels at 80 km/h and a bike at 60 km/h in the same direction. The bike starts 30 minutes before the car. How long after the car starts does it catch the bike?
items.explanation: In 30 minutes the bike covers 30 km. The car gains 20 km/h on the bike, so it needs 30/20 = 1.5 hours to close the gap.

items.question: Tea costing Rs 40 per kg is mixed with tea costing Rs 60 per kg in the ratio 3:2. What is the cost price of the mixture per kg?
items.explanation: The cost is (3 x 40 + 2 x 60)/5 = 240/5 = Rs 48 per kg. The mixture price is a weighted average, weighted by the ratio 3:2, not a simple average of 50.

items.question: What is the value of log5(125)?
items.explanation: 5^3 = 125, so log base 5 of 125 is 3. A logarithm asks for the exponent, and 5 raised to 3 is 125.

items.question: What is the total surface area of a cuboid of length 4 cm, breadth 5 cm and height 6 cm?
items.explanation: Surface area is 2(lb + bh + hl) = 2(20 + 30 + 24) = 2 x 74 = 148 sq cm. A cuboid has three pairs of equal faces, hence the factor of 2.

items.question: Which film sold the most tickets in total over the four weeks?

diagram.caption: Tickets sold (thousands) for four films, Week 1 to Week 4

items.explanation: Adding the four weeks: A = 300, B = 305, C = 260, D = 290 thousand. Film B sold the most at 305 thousand tickets.

items.question: What is the percentage growth in Film A's ticket sales from Week 1 to Week 4?
items.explanation: Film A's sales rose from 60 thousand in Week 1 to 90 thousand in Week 4, an increase of 30 thousand. The percentage growth is 30/60 x 100 = 50%.

items.question: In which week were the combined ticket sales of all four films the highest, and by how much did they exceed the lowest week?
items.explanation: The combined totals are Week 1 = 270, Week 2 = 285, Week 3 = 285 and Week 4 = 315 thousand. The highest is Week 4 at 315 and the lowest is Week 1 at 270, so Week 4 exceeds Week 1 by 45 thousand.

items.question: What is the overall percentage increase in total visitors from 2023 to 2024?
items.explanation: Total visitors in 2023 were 1300 thousand and in 2024 they were 1405 thousand. The increase is 105 on a base of 1300, which is 8.1%.

items.question: Which museum recorded the highest percentage growth in visitors?
items.explanation: Growth rates are: M1 15.0%, M2 10.0%, M3 20.0%, M4 -10.0%. M3 has the highest percentage growth at 20.0%.

items.question: What is the ratio of M1 visitors to M2 visitors in 2024?
items.explanation: In 2024 M1 had 460 thousand visitors and M2 had 330 thousand, so the ratio is 460:330. Dividing both sides by 10 gives 46:33.

items.question: Which is the national animal of India?
items.explanation: The Bengal tiger is the national animal of India. The Asiatic lion is found in Gir, the Indian elephant is the national heritage animal, and the one-horned rhinoceros is found in Assam.

items.question: Who built the Red Fort in Delhi?
items.explanation: Shah Jahan built the Red Fort in Delhi in the 1640s. Akbar built the Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri, Babur founded the Mughal Empire, and Aurangzeb built the Bibi Ka Maqbara.

items.question: What is the currency of the United Kingdom?
items.explanation: The United Kingdom uses the pound sterling. The euro is used in the Eurozone, the dollar in the United States, and the franc in Switzerland and parts of Africa.

items.question: Which is the largest desert in the world?
items.explanation: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world. The Gobi is in Asia, the Kalahari in southern Africa, and the Arabian desert is smaller than the Sahara.

items.question: Who founded Microsoft along with Paul Allen?
items.explanation: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft with Paul Allen in 1975. Steve Jobs founded Apple, Jeff Bezos founded Amazon, and Larry Page founded Google.

items.question: The headquarters of UNESCO is located in which city?
items.explanation: UNESCO is headquartered in Paris, France. Geneva hosts the WHO, New York hosts the UN, and Rome hosts the FAO.

items.question: Who wrote 'Wings of Fire'?
items.explanation: A P J Abdul Kalam wrote 'Wings of Fire', his autobiography, published in 1999. Vikram Sarabhai founded the space programme, Homi Bhabha founded atomic energy, and Satish Dhawan led ISRO.

items.question: Which is the highest peak in India?
items.explanation: Kangchenjunga, at 8,586 metres, is the highest peak in India. Nanda Devi is the second highest wholly within India, Everest lies on the Nepal-China border, and K2 lies in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

items.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the right to equality?
items.explanation: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. Article 19 lists freedoms, Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, and Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies.

items.question: The First War of Indian Independence took place in which year?
items.explanation: The First War of Indian Independence, or the revolt of 1857, began in 1857. The Quit India Movement was in 1942, and the Swadeshi Movement began in 1905.

items.question: Who developed the periodic table of elements?
items.explanation: Dmitri Mendeleev published the periodic table in 1869. John Dalton proposed atomic theory, Niels Bohr proposed the atomic model, and Marie Curie worked on radioactivity.

items.question: Which Indian state is the largest producer of tea?
items.explanation: Assam is the largest producer of tea in India. West Bengal is second, Kerala and Tamil Nadu produce tea on a smaller scale.

items.question: The headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization is located in which city?
items.explanation: The FAO is headquartered in Rome, Italy. Geneva hosts the WHO, Paris hosts UNESCO, and Vienna hosts the IAEA.

items.question: Which river is known as the 'Sorrow of Bengal'?
items.explanation: The Damodar is called the Sorrow of Bengal because of its destructive floods. The Hooghly is a distributary of the Ganga, the Teesta flows through Sikkim and Bengal, and the Mahanadi flows through Odisha.

items.question: Who was the first Indian to win an individual Olympic gold medal?
items.explanation: Abhinav Bindra won gold in shooting at the Beijing Olympics in 2008, the first individual Olympic gold for India. Leander Paes won a bronze in 1996, Rathore won a silver in 2004, and Malleswari won a bronze in 2000.

items.question: Which scheme provides 100 days of guaranteed wage employment in rural India?
items.explanation: MGNREGA, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, guarantees 100 days of wage employment a year to rural households. PM-KISAN gives income support to farmers, PM-JAY is health insurance, and Stand-Up India supports loans for entrepreneurs.

items.question: The 'Rowlatt Act' was passed in which year?
items.explanation: The Rowlatt Act was passed in 1919, allowing detention without trial, and it led to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. The Government of India Act was passed in 1935.

items.question: Which is the largest producer of cotton in India?
items.explanation: Gujarat is the largest producer of cotton in India. Maharashtra is second, Punjab and Telangana are smaller producers.

items.question: Who wrote 'My Experiments with Truth'?
items.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi wrote 'My Experiments with Truth', his autobiography. Nehru wrote 'The Discovery of India', Tagore wrote 'Gitanjali', and Patel did not write an autobiography of this name.

items.question: The 'Ryotwari system' of land revenue was introduced by which British administrator?
items.explanation: Thomas Munro introduced the Ryotwari system in the Madras Presidency, settling revenue directly with cultivators. Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement, Hastings was the first Governor-General, and Wellesley introduced the Subsidiary Alliance.

items.question: Which schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha?
items.explanation: The Fourth Schedule allocates seats in the Rajya Sabha to the states and union territories. The Third Schedule contains oaths, the Fifth Schedule deals with scheduled areas, and the Sixth Schedule deals with tribal areas in the Northeast.

items.question: The 'Subsidiary Alliance' system was introduced by which Governor-General?
items.explanation: Lord Wellesley introduced the Subsidiary Alliance, under which Indian rulers accepted British troops and paid for them. Dalhousie introduced the Doctrine of Lapse, Cornwallis the Permanent Settlement, and Hastings the policy of paramountcy.

items.question: Which country hosted the COP28 climate summit in 2023?
items.explanation: COP28 was held in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, in 2023. Egypt hosted COP27, Scotland hosted COP26, and Brazil hosted COP30.

items.question: The first census of India was conducted in which year?
items.explanation: The first census of India was conducted in 1872 under Lord Mayo. The first complete and synchronous census was in 1881, and the first census after independence was in 1951.

items.question: Which Indian state was the first to introduce the mid-day meal scheme in schools?
items.explanation: Tamil Nadu pioneered the mid-day meal scheme, introduced by K Kamaraj in the 1950s and expanded by M G Ramachandran in the 1980s. Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka adopted it later.
